short: The Treason Act 1534 expanded the definition of high treason to include spoken words against the King, his titles, or his marriage.
full:
Following the Act of Supremacy, which declared Henry VIII the Supreme Head of the Church of England, Parliament passed the Treason Act 1534 to enforce compliance. It radically expanded the scope of high treason, which had previously been restricted largely to overt actions such as levying war against the monarch or plotting their death. Under the new law, merely speaking against the King, depriving him of his titles, or calling him a heretic, schismatic, or tyrant was sufficient for a treason conviction.

This legislation criminalised dissent during a period of profound religious and political upheaval. It provided the legal framework for the executions of high-profile opponents of the Reformation, including Thomas More and John Fisher, who had refused to acknowledge Henry's supremacy. The Act established a climate of fear and demonstrated the formidable coercive power of the Henrician state.
